title: Night Feeds and Sleep
summary:
A baby waking at night to feed is a real need, not a bad habit or spoiling; in the first months they need to feed often, night and day. The World Health Organization recommends breastfeeding on demand, as often as the baby wants, night and day. Night feeds help the mother's milk supply, and breast milk protects the baby from infections and lowers the risk of sudden infant death.

Learn your baby's hunger signs before they cry: putting their hands to their mouth, turning their head towards the breast or bottle, or licking their lips; crying is a late sign of hunger. Not every cry is hunger; they may need a cuddle or a clean nappy. In the first weeks some newborns are sleepy and do not ask to feed, so ask the doctor or nurse whether you should wake your baby to feed.

Keep night feeds calm: dim lights, few words in a quiet voice, no play, and no nappy change unless needed, then put them back in their cot on their back. If they are bottle-fed, hold them semi-upright, never leave them alone with a propped-up bottle, and never leave them in bed with a bottle, as they may choke on the milk.

If you fear you might fall asleep while feeding, do not feed on a sofa or armchair. If you bring your baby into your bed to feed, keep pillows and covers away from them, and put them back in their own cot before you sleep, or as soon as you wake if you do fall asleep. Never bring them into your bed at all if either of you smokes, has had alcohol, drugs or medicine that makes you drowsy, or if your baby was born prematurely or with a low birth weight.

As they grow, night feeds usually become fewer, and some babies between six months and a year may no longer need them, while others still wake from hunger or teething pain. There is no single age to stop them: follow your baby's hunger signs, and ask the doctor before cutting them down, or if you are worried about their feeding or weight. If, when you try to wake them, they are hard to wake or will not wake, are floppy in an unusual way, have difficulty breathing or stop breathing, turn blue or grey, or have a temperature of 38C or higher while under three months old or 39C or higher while aged three to six months, call an ambulance or go to the emergency department straight away. You will find the other signs, such as a low temperature and a rash, in the lesson «Signs That Cannot Wait Until Morning».
try_this: Today: Set up your night-feeding spot: a dim light within reach, a place that is not a sofa or armchair, and your baby's cot close by so you can put them back on their back after every feed.
reflection_prompts: Where do night feeds usually happen, and what could you change so they stay safe for your baby if you fall asleep?
